Thanks again for taking this. We're starting the architecture review for Horizon's private deployment (we're aiming for a VPC-backed Redwood Private install in our AWS account). High-level asks:

- We need guidance on whether to use VPC peering, AWS PrivateLink, or a site-to-site VPN to connect our app fleet to Redwood's inference endpoints.
- Main constraints: strict egress control (no public internet to inference), PCI-adjacent environment, and a mix of steady production traffic plus occasional large-batch uploads for offline processing.
- Latency goal for tail p50/p95 under 50ms/150ms within us-east-1; cross-region not in scope for initial rollout.

Samara — thanks for the context and the diagram, helpful. Looping in Karthik and Marcus for the deep network implications. High-level guidance up front:

- PrivateLink (AWS) gives you the tightest egress control and per-account endpoint management; it's good when you require no cross-account peering and want to restrict traffic to a service endpoint. However, it does add per-endpoint ENI costs and can complicate cross-AZ high-availability if not architected carefully.

- VPC Peering has lower steady-state latency and no per-request NATing, but it requires route table management and doesn't support transitive routing. It's straightforward for single-account-to-single-account setups in the same region. Peering across AWS Organizations can be policy-limited and isn't ideal if you want to keep the service logically isolated.

- Site-to-site VPN is fastest to stand up, works across networks/accounts, and can be configured with strict controls, but it's more operationally heavy (BGP, key rotation, possible throughput limits) and generally has higher latency/variability than PrivateLink or peering. For bulk data uploads it can be a good fallback.

Can you confirm:
1) Will Horizon manage the AWS account where Redwood Private will be deployed, or will Redwood run customer-managed connectors from our side?
2) Do you need all inference traffic to stay within Horizon-owned VPC subnets (i.e., no Egress to any managed Redwood subnet)?

I'll attach a simple comparison matrix with perf/ops/cost heuristics.

— Hannah

Hi all — quick note from field ops perspective:

- If Horizon's security team requires granular IP-level allowlists and you want to avoid shared VPC-level trust, PrivateLink is often the cleanest. It forces an explicit endpoint per-service and keeps your route tables tidy.

- For high-throughput bulk transfers (model artifacts, large embeddings), a dedicated S2S VPN with route-based BGP and MTU tuning will outperform a PrivateLink endpoint for sustained bandwidth; PrivateLink can throttle depending on how the service is backed.

- Peering gives you the lowest RTT in-region but remember that peering requires both sides to accept routes and manage CIDR overlaps — we commonly see customers need to re-IP before peering. Also: cross-account peering can be problematic if you plan for future org-level isolation.

I'll add that hybrid is a viable pattern: PrivateLink for API/real-time inference calls (strict egress control), and S2S for admin/bulk flows (CI/CD, artifact sync). That keeps low-latency paths for critical inference while giving you a controlled bulk channel.

Liam
Principal Network Architect, NetBridge (contractor)

Samara / team — digging into specifics against Horizon's diagram:

- Latency: For same-region traffic (us-east-1), VPC peering will consistently give you the best p50/p95 numbers for RPC-style inference calls because it avoids extra proxying. Expect baseline p50 in single-digit ms internal-only; p95 depends on bursting patterns. If you need strict tenant isolation and auditable flows, PrivateLink adds an ENI hop but we usually see acceptable added latency (~2-8ms) if endpoints are spread across AZs.

- Throughput & cost: S2S VPN has both throughput caps (depending on vendor and encryption) and potential egress data charges; PrivateLink incurs an endpoint-hour and data-processing fee; peering has near-zero per-GB charges inside the same region (aside from inter-AZ data transfer in some cases). We'll model costs once you confirm expected token rate / MB per request.

- Security/compliance: PrivateLink gives you the strongest control surface for preventing unwanted outbound egress, since traffic terminates at an interface endpoint in your account. With peering, you share a routing plane and must enforce access via security groups and NACLs. For PCI-adjacent workloads, customers often prefer PrivateLink + endpoint policies to meet scoping requirements.

- Operational constraints: If Horizon wants Redwood to host a customer-managed VPC (we run connectors in your VPC), peering is straightforward. If Horizon must own all subnets and control auditing, PrivateLink is better because it doesn't require us to sit inside your network.

Recommendation (short):
1) Primary: PrivateLink for API traffic (real-time inference) — meets egress control and compliance needs.
2) Secondary: Site-to-site VPN for bulk admin/batch sync and as a fallback route during incidents.
3) Avoid peering today unless Horizon is comfortable with tight CIDR management and wants the absolute lowest latency; re-evaluate after initial rollout.

I've attached a draft MCA redlines doc with suggested wording on connectivity responsibilities and who pays for endpoints/links. Also included a quick checklist for Firewall rules, MTU, and BGP settings if you pick S2S.

Karthik
